hook: Every few years the news fills with layoffs, store closings and worried shoppers; a few years later it is help-wanted signs and rising prices. These swings are the business cycle. Behind them is a steadier line, the economy's potential output, and the distance between the two, the output gap, tells you whether to expect rising unemployment or rising inflation.

options: Unemployment caused by a fall in total spending and output
People who have stopped looking for work
prereq.why: Cyclical unemployment comes from downturns; it equals the actual rate minus the natural rate.

prereq.q: Why does real GDP, not nominal GDP, show changes in output?
options: It holds prices at base-year levels
It is measured in current prices
prereq.why: Real GDP values output at base-year prices, so it changes only with quantities produced.

figure.caption: Real GDP rises in expansions and falls in contractions around potential output, which grows over time; the distance between them is the output gap.

chain.cause: Total spending in the economy falls
chain.effect: firms sell less, cut production and real GDP falls: a contraction

chain.cause: Real GDP falls below potential output
chain.effect: there is a negative (recessionary) output gap
cyclical unemployment rises and the unemployment rate goes above the natural rate

chain.cause: Later, real GDP rises above potential in a boom
chain.effect: unemployment falls below the natural rate and inflation tends to rise

ideas: The business cycle has two phases, expansion (real GDP rising) and contraction (real GDP falling). The peak and trough are the turning points.
Potential output is real GDP at full employment (the natural rate of unemployment). It grows over time.
Output gap = real GDP - potential output. Negative (recessionary): cyclical unemployment. Positive (inflationary): unemployment below the natural rate and rising inflation.
A recession is a severe, lasting contraction. On a PPC, a recession is a point inside the curve; potential output is a point on it.

misconception.wrong: Peak and trough are phases of the business cycle, and potential output is the most an economy can ever produce.
misconception.right: The phases are expansion and contraction; peak and trough are the turning points. Potential output is the sustainable full-employment level, and real GDP can rise above it for a while in a boom.

summary: Real GDP rises in expansions and falls in contractions around potential output, the full-employment level that grows over time. The output gap is real GDP minus potential: a negative (recessionary) gap brings cyclical unemployment, and a positive (inflationary) gap brings unemployment below the natural rate and rising inflation. Peak and trough are the turning points between the phases.
